To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the N-methyl-D-asparatic acid (NMDA) receptor antagonist MK-851 impairs learning but does not disrupt the fixation or expression of a classically conditioned fear response in goldfish.

NMDA receptors are involved in the learning process but not the memory fixation or expression process for the acquisition of BSR conditioning in goldfish, and that the NMDA-dependent process is involved in the learning of the conditioned and unconditioned BSRs.
the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-81 produces anterograde, but not retrograde amnesia for the acquisition of a conditioned fear response in goldfish.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of MK-801 on learning and memory in a simple, visually mediated, associative learning paradigm.
the neurobiological mechanisms that underlie the acquisition of conditioned fear responses.
the role of N-methyl-D-asparatic acid (NMDA) receptors in classical fear conditioning in fish.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NMDA receptor antagonist MK- 801 impairs learning, but not memory fixation, of a classical conditioned BSR in goldfish.
MK-801 does impair the learning of a conditioned branchial suppression response in goldfish but not its memory fixation and/or expression.
MK-801 produces anterograde but not retrograde amnesia and does not produce state dependency in goldfish BSR conditioning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NMDA receptor antagonists impair learning but not memory in the goldfish.
MK-801 impaires the acquisition of BSR conditioning in goldfish, but does not affect the expression of the learned response.
N-methyl-D-asparate receptor blockade impairs learning but does not impair memory fixation or expression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MK-801 imparts anterograde, but not retrograde or state-dependent, amnesia in goldfish, which is similar to the results of other studies on mammals.

MK-801 produces amnesia for BSR conditioning by interfering with the learning of the conditioned branchial suppression response (CBSR) but does not affect the expression of the CBSR once it has been learned.
MK-801 imparts a selective impairment in learning and does not disrupt the expression of conditioned and unconditioned BSRs.
